points.point: The author embraces the motto that the best government governs least, and ultimately believes the best government governs not at all, once men are prepared for it.

Majorities rule because they are physically strongest, not because they are right or fair, so majority rule in all cases cannot rest on justice; majorities should decide only questions of expediency, and conscience should decide right and wrong.
The citizen should not resign his conscience to the legislator: we should be men first and subjects afterward, respecting the right more than the law, and bound only to do what he thinks right.
The author cannot recognize as his government one that is also the slave's government, and he cannot without disgrace be associated with it.

All men recognize the right of revolution against unendurable tyranny; minor evils may be tolerated as machine friction, but when oppression and robbery are organized, as with slavery and the unjust conquest of Mexico by an invading American army, honest men should rebel.

Paley reduces civil obligation to expediency, but ignores cases where justice must be done at any cost, like restoring a plank taken from a drowning man, so the nation must cease holding slaves and warring on Mexico even at the cost of its existence.
Voting is a form of gaming with right and wrong that does not stake one's character, leaves right to the majority, and amounts to doing nothing for it.
A man is not bound to devote himself to eradicating every wrong, but he must at least withdraw his own practical support from it and not live at another's expense.

If injustice is merely part of the machine's friction one may let it be, but if it requires you to be the agent of injustice to another, you should break the law and make your life a counter friction, refusing to lend yourself to the wrong you condemn.

Abolitionists should withdraw their support, in person and property, from the Massachusetts government without waiting for a majority, since anyone more right than his neighbors is already a majority of one.
Under a government that imprisons anyone unjustly, the true place for a just man is prison, which the author calls the only honorable place for a free man in a slave state.

A minority is powerless while it conforms but irresistible when it clogs the machinery with its whole weight, and the State would have to choose between jailing all just men and giving up war and slavery.
He concluded the State was half-witted and timid, lost his respect for it and pitied it, since it confronts only a man's body and relies on physical strength rather than wit or honesty.

Because the State's force is partly human, appeal is possible to its makers and to the people themselves, and it can be resisted with effect, unlike fire or nature, so he does not resign himself to things as they are.
Government authority, even that which he is willing to submit to, is impure unless it has the sanction and consent of the governed.
There will never be a truly free and enlightened State until it recognizes the individual as a higher, independent power from which all its own authority derives, and treats him accordingly.
The author imagines a State that is just to all, respects the individual as a neighbor, and tolerates a few living aloof from it while fulfilling their duties as neighbors and fellow-men.
